title: Language Models Are Unsupervised Multitask Learners
headline: A model trained only to predict the next word, on text diverse enough that tasks show up inside it, learns to do those tasks with no extra training just by being asked in plain language, and it does this better the bigger it gets.
abstract: Natural language processing tasks, such as question answering, machine translation, reading comprehension, and summarization, are typically approached with supervised learning on task-specific datasets. We demonstrate that language models begin to learn these tasks without any explicit supervision when trained on a new dataset of millions of webpages called WebText. When conditioned on a document plus questions, the answers generated by the language model reach 55 F1 on the CoQA dataset - matching or exceeding the performance of 3 out of 4 baseline systems without using the 127,000+ training examples. The capacity of the language model is essential to the success of zero-shot task transfer and increasing it improves performance in a log-linear fashion across tasks. Our largest model, GPT-2, is a 1.5B parameter Transformer that achieves state of the art results on 7 out of 8 tested language modeling datasets in a zero-shot setting but still underfits WebText. Samples from the model reflect these improvements and contain coherent paragraphs of text. These findings suggest a promising path towards building language processing systems which learn to perform tasks from their naturally occurring demonstrations.

images.alt: A clay-orange pixel reader sits with an open book between a sage scroll of stacked web pages feeding in from the left and three ink tags fanning out to the right labelled answer, know, and any, showing that one reader of the whole internet can answer any kind of question without being taught the task.
images.caption: Read enough of everything and the tasks fall out for free, no task-specific training needed.

images.alt: A row of blank pixel word tiles runs left to right with the last filled tile glowing clay-orange and a dashed empty slot for the next word, while a sage fan of three candidate tiles points down at the slot with arrows of different thickness and the thickest one winning, showing the model works by guessing the next word over and over.
images.caption: The whole engine is one move repeated: score every candidate next word, then pick one.

images.alt: A clay-orange pixel reader has two paper tags labelled hint taped to its input, the top tag leading to a summary scrap and the bottom tag leading to a sage question-and-answer scrap, showing that a short plain-language hint in the prompt tells the same model which task to do.
images.caption: The same model becomes a summarizer or a question answerer depending on the few words you put in the prompt.

images.alt: Four pixel readers grow taller from left to right, sage and small on the left up to a tall glowing clay-orange one on the right, with an ink trend arrow sweeping up across them and axis ticks beneath labelled smaller model and more free tasks, showing that a bigger model does more tasks zero-shot in a steady log-linear climb.
images.caption: Bigger model, more tasks for free; the gains rise log-linearly with size.
